topics.title: Introduction, Meaning and Need of Standard Costing
explain: Cost control is a primary objective of cost management using predetermined costs.
A standard cost is a planned unit cost established before starting production.
Standard costing sets targets, measures actual costs, and reports variances for prompt management action.
It assists management in decision-making, budgeting, inventory valuation, and fixing product prices.
topics.example: Setting a target cost of ₹50 per dish before catering an event, then checking actual expenditure after service.
remember: CIMA defines Standard Cost as a planned unit cost of a product or service produced in a period.
mistakes: Confusing standard costing with historical costing, which only records past actual expenses without preset targets.

quiz.q: What is standard costing primarily used for in an organisation?
o: Cost control and performance evaluation through variance analysis
Calculating tax liabilities at year end
quiz.why: Standard costing compares actual costs against pre-set standards to identify variances for performance control.

quiz.q: Standard cost is best described as:
o: Actual cost incurred at the end of production
Historical average cost of past 5 years
Planned unit cost determined on pre-set bases
quiz.why: CIMA defines standard cost as the planned unit cost of a product or service determined in advance.

topics.title: Types of Standards
explain: Ideal Standards represent maximum efficiency under perfect operating conditions, but are practically unattainable.
Normal Standards are targets achievable under normal operating conditions averaged over a longer cycle.
Basic or Bogey Standards remain constant over long periods to establish long-term trends.
Current Standards reflect management expectations of actual costs for the current operating period.
topics.example: Aiming for 100% test marks with zero study breaks is an ideal standard, while targeting 80% based on daily routine is a current standard.
remember: When basic standards are used, variances are generally not calculated; actual cost is expressed as a percentage of basic cost.
mistakes: Using ideal standards for worker evaluation, which demotivates staff because variances are always adverse and unattainable.

quiz.q: Which type of standard remains unaltered over a very long period to establish cost trends?
quiz.why: Basic standards are set on a long-term basis, seldom revised, and serve as base year points.

quiz.q: Ideal standards are often criticized because:
o: They are too easy to achieve
They are based on old historical data
They are unattainable and demotivating for workers
quiz.why: Ideal standards assume perfect conditions with zero waste, making them practically unattainable.

topics.title: Setting Physical and Price/Rate Standards
explain: Setting standard costs requires establishing physical quantity standards and price/rate standards.
Material physical standards involve product studies, specification lists, and experimental test runs.
Labour time standards rely on time-and-motion studies, machine layout, and worker training levels.
Material price standards consider current stocks, existing purchase contracts, market trends, and minimum support prices.

flow.title: Procedure to Set Material Quantity Standards

topics.example: Determining exact flour required per loaf of bread by conducting test bakes in a commercial bakery.
remember: Time and motion studies are conducted by industrial engineers to set accurate standard labour hours.
mistakes: Ignoring normal expected wastage when setting physical quantity and labour time standards.

quiz.q: Which technique is specifically used to determine standard labour time for a job?
quiz.why: Time and motion studies analyze job operations to determine the standard time an average worker requires.

quiz.q: Material price standards are primarily formulated with input from which department?
quiz.why: The purchasing department has expert knowledge of current market prices, supplier terms, and price trends.

topics.title: Classification and Types of Variances
explain: A variance is the difference between standard performance and actual performance.
Controllable Variances can be regulated by a responsibility centre under normal working conditions.
Uncontrollable Variances occur due to factors outside managerial control like market price surges or laws.
Favourable Variance (F) means actual cost is less than standard cost; Adverse Variance (A) means actual cost exceeds standard cost.
topics.example: Spending ₹90 when standard budget was ₹100 creates a Favourable Variance of ₹10 (F).
remember: Favourable cost variance = Actual Cost < Standard Cost; Adverse cost variance = Actual Cost > Standard Cost.
mistakes: Assuming mathematical plus (+) or minus (-) signs always align directly with Favourable or Adverse without checking cost context.

quiz.q: A variance is classified as 'Adverse' for a cost component when:
o: Actual cost is less than standard cost
quiz.why: In cost accounting, an adverse variance occurs when actual expenses are higher than predetermined standards.

quiz.q: Uncontrollable variances are those which arise due to:
o: External economic factors beyond managerial control
quiz.why: Uncontrollable variances stem from external changes like market price fluctuations or policy shifts.

topics.title: Direct Material Cost Variances
explain: Material Cost Variance (MCV) = Standard Material Cost for Actual Production - Actual Material Cost.
Material Price Variance (MPV) = Actual Quantity x (Standard Price - Actual Price).
Material Usage Variance (MUV) = Standard Price x (Standard Quantity - Actual Quantity).
MUV further splits into Material Mix Variance (MMV) and Material Yield Variance (MYV) when multiple materials are mixed.
topics.example: If standard steel required for actual output is 100 kg at ₹10/kg and actual used is 120 kg at ₹10/kg, MUV is ₹200 (A).
remember: Standard Quantity (SQ) must ALWAYS be adjusted to reflect the Standard Quantity allowed for ACTUAL output produced.
mistakes: Using original budgeted output quantity as SQ directly instead of calculating SQ for actual output achieved.

quiz.q: What is the formula for Material Price Variance (MPV)?
o: Standard Price x (Standard Quantity - Actual Quantity)
Actual Quantity x (Standard Price - Actual Price)
Standard Quantity x (Standard Price - Actual Price)
Actual Price x (Standard Quantity - Actual Quantity)
quiz.why: MPV isolates the price deviation per unit over the total actual quantity purchased or used: AQ x (SP - AP).

quiz.q: Material Usage Variance (MUV) is equal to:
o: Material Price Variance + Material Cost Variance
Material Mix Variance + Material Yield Variance
Material Yield Variance - Material Price Variance
quiz.why: MUV measures total quantitative deviation, which subdivides into mix proportion changes (MMV) and yield efficiency (MYV).

topics.title: Direct Labour Cost Variances
explain: Labour Cost Variance (LCV) = (Standard Hours x Standard Rate) - (Actual Hours Paid x Actual Rate).
Labour Rate Variance (LRV) = Actual Hours Paid x (Standard Rate - Actual Rate).
Labour Efficiency Variance (LEV) = Standard Rate x (Standard Hours - Actual Hours Worked).
Idle Time Variance = Abnormal Idle Hours x Standard Rate (This is ALWAYS Adverse).
LEV splits into Labour Mix (Gang) Variance and Labour Yield Variance.

flow.title: Labour Variance Analysis Steps
steps: Calculate Rate Variance on Paid Hours
Calculate Efficiency Variance on Worked Hours
Divide Efficiency into Mix and Yield

topics.example: Workers paid for 50 hours at ₹20/hr complete work in 45 hours; the 5 hours saved yield a Favourable Efficiency Variance of ₹100 (F).
remember: Idle time variance is calculated on idle hours using Standard Rate and is ALWAYS adverse.
mistakes: Using actual hours paid instead of actual hours worked when calculating Labour Efficiency Variance.

quiz.q: Which labour variance is ALWAYS adverse in nature?
quiz.why: Idle time represents paid unproductive hours, leading strictly to a loss (Adverse variance).

quiz.q: Labour Efficiency Variance is calculated based on:
quiz.why: Efficiency evaluates productivity during active work, so actual hours worked are compared against standard hours.

topics.title: Variable Overhead Cost Variances
explain: Variable Overhead Cost Variance (VOCV) = Standard Variable Overhead for Actual Production - Actual Variable Overhead.
VOCV = (Standard Hours for Actual Output x Standard Rate per hour) - Actual Variable Overhead.
Variable Overhead Expenditure Variance = Actual Hours Worked x (Standard Rate - Actual Rate).
Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance = Standard Rate x (Standard Hours for Actual Output - Actual Hours Worked).
topics.example: Working 11,600 hours at a standard variable rate of ₹10/hr with actual expense ₹1,22,000 gives an Expenditure Variance of ₹6,000 (A).
remember: Variable overheads generally vary with labour hours or machine hours worked unless specified otherwise.
mistakes: Confusing standard variable overhead rate per unit with standard variable overhead rate per hour.

quiz.q: Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance formula is:
o: Standard Rate x (Standard Hours - Actual Hours Worked)
Actual Hours x (Standard Rate - Actual Rate)
Standard Rate x (Budgeted Hours - Actual Hours)
Actual Rate x (Standard Hours - Actual Hours)
quiz.why: Efficiency variance measures hours saved/lost at standard rate: Standard Rate x (SH - AH Worked).

quiz.q: Total Variable Overhead Cost Variance equals:
quiz.why: Variable overhead cost variance splits into spending (expenditure) and hours efficiency components.

topics.title: Fixed Overhead Cost Variances
explain: Fixed Overhead Cost Variance (FOCV) = Absorbed Fixed Overhead - Actual Fixed Overhead.
Fixed Overhead Expenditure Variance = Budgeted Fixed Overhead - Actual Fixed Overhead.
Fixed Overhead Volume Variance = Absorbed Fixed Overhead - Budgeted Fixed Overhead.
Volume Variance subdivides into Efficiency Variance, Capacity Variance, and Calendar Variance (when actual days differ from budgeted days).
topics.example: Absorbing ₹1,53,090 overhead on actual production against budgeted ₹1,50,000 yields a Favourable Volume Variance of ₹3,090 (F).
remember: Absorbed Fixed Overhead = Standard Hours for Actual Production x Standard Fixed Overhead Rate per hour.
mistakes: Forgetting to compute Revised Budgeted Hours when actual working days differ from budgeted working days.

quiz.why: Volume variance reflects under/over recovery due to output variation: Absorbed Overhead - Budgeted Overhead.

quiz.q: Which variance arises when actual working days differ from standard budgeted working days?
quiz.why: Calendar variance isolates the impact of extra or lost working days on fixed overhead absorption.

topics.title: Advantages and Criticism of Standard Costing
explain: Advantages include effective cost control, realistic pricing, performance evaluation, and Management by Exception.
Management by Exception allows managers to focus only on significant adverse or favourable variances.
Criticisms center around difficult price predictions, rapid technological changes, and high setup costs for small firms.
Standards must be regularly updated to remain meaningful and effective for operational control.
topics.example: A manager reviewing only cost items that deviate by more than 5% from standard budget (Management by Exception).
remember: Standards are not permanent; they require periodic revision when market prices or production technology change.
mistakes: Assuming basic standards alone are adequate for current cost control without updating them.

quiz.q: What does 'Management by Exception' mean in standard costing?
o: Managing all operations without any budgets
Focusing executive attention only on significant cost deviations
quiz.why: Management by exception saves time by highlighting only abnormal variances that require corrective action.

quiz.q: Standard costing may be less effective in industries characterized by:
o: Stable raw material prices and long production runs
Frequent rapid technological changes and custom job orders
Standardized mass production of single product
quiz.why: Frequent changes in technology and job-type custom work make standard setting difficult and quickly outdated.
